source_batch.unit_label: ABFM Module C unit 5 (courseware unit 17): mergers, acquisitions and restructuring

facts.statement: Types of transactions (courseware): a merger is the coming together of two businesses into one, usually with the combined business larger afterwards. Types: horizontal (same market, more market share, possible near-monopoly), vertical (buyer-seller relationship), conglomerate (completely unconnected lines of business; goals are use of financial resources, more debt capacity and managerial integration), congeneric (connected through technology, products or markets), and reverse (a smaller unlisted company acquires a larger listed one, letting the unlisted firm avoid a lengthy public issue). An acquisition is the purchase of a controlling interest in the shares of an existing firm (by agreement with the majority holder, fresh shares, open market purchase, partly in cash and partly in shares, or a general offer to shareholders); the acquired firm may keep running as a separate company or be combined. A slump sale transfers a business for a single lump sum without values for individual assets. A purchase of a division or plant takes over only part of a firm assets and liabilities. A takeover is the acquisition of a specified stake (typically 50 to 100 per cent) giving control, friendly if the target management agrees and hostile if not. A leveraged buyout is a takeover or purchase of a division financed largely by debt.

Divestitures (courseware): where acquisitions add control and asset base, divestitures shrink them. Types: a partial sell-off (one company sells part of its operations to another), transfer of ownership (an investor sells an equity stake or controlling block), a demerger (a company transfers one or more businesses to another company formed for the purpose, with the transferring company the demerged company and the receiving one the resulting company), an equity carve-out (a parent sells part of its holding in a wholly owned subsidiary to the public or a strategic investor), and public sector disinvestment (transfer of government ownership through privatisation, partial or complete).

Reasons for mergers (courseware): synergy, where the combined value exceeds the separate values, V(AB) > V(A) + V(B); operating economies from complementary services and economies of scale (real economies reduce factor inputs per unit of output; pecuniary economies come from cheaper factor prices); tax benefits such as set-off of losses; faster growth than organic growth, with a shorter time to market; consolidation of production capacity and market power; economies of scope; vertical integration economies (though outsourcing may sometimes be better); complementary resources; use of surplus funds; managerial effectiveness (a better team replaces a weaker one, and the threat of takeover disciplines managers); and industry consolidation where there are too many players or too much capacity.

Dubious reasons for mergers (courseware): diversification to cut risk adds no value to investors who can diversify cheaply by holding shares in both companies, with two exceptions (a firm threatened with bankruptcy that can be saved only by merger, and a firm whose owners cannot diversify by themselves). Lower financing costs: a merged firm may borrow more cheaply, but the creditors of each firm become a guarantor of the other, so the shareholders of each bear extra risk and in an efficient market the lower cost of debt is offset by the higher cost of equity, with no net gain. Growth in earnings per share: if the market is efficient the price-earnings ratio of the combined firm falls so that its market value is the sum of the separate values, and the earnings per share growth is an illusion; only an inefficient market could be fooled.

Mechanics of an amalgamation (courseware): the Companies Act is the main legislation, SEBI is concerned with minority shareholders, the Competition Commission with consumers harmed by reduced competition. Steps in sequence: review of the object clauses of both memoranda to confirm the merger is permitted; communication with the stock exchanges; board approvals of the draft scheme; application to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT); notice with an explanatory statement to shareholders and creditors; separate meetings of shareholders and creditors in which a prescribed majority in value must approve; a petition to the NCLT to confirm the scheme; filing the order with the Registrar of Companies; transfer of the assets and liabilities of the merging company to the merged business as at the appointed date; and issue of shares and debentures of the merged company, after which the stock exchange begins trading. The courseware states specific majorities, notice periods and thresholds which are not taught here. Competition approval: a combination that has an appreciable adverse effect on competition in India can be investigated by the Commission, and proposed combinations above specified limits must be notified to it.

Tax and accounting (courseware): an amalgamation may qualify for tax benefits where all the properties and liabilities of the amalgamating company pass to the amalgamated company and a required proportion of its shareholders become shareholders of the amalgamated company; the combined firm can then claim certain deductions and carry forward unabsorbed losses and depreciation (the figures and sections are not taught). Stamp duty is levied by the states. Accounting for business combinations under Ind AS 103 uses the acquisition method: identify the acquirer, determine the acquisition date, recognise and measure the identifiable assets acquired, liabilities assumed and any non-controlling interest, and recognise goodwill or a gain from a bargain purchase. Business combinations under common control (all combining entities ultimately controlled by the same party before and after) use the pooling of interests method: assets and liabilities are recorded at carrying amounts, no fair value adjustments are made, and the difference in capital caused by the share exchange is adjusted in reserves.

Role of investment bankers (courseware): they arrange mergers (through an M&A group that finds targets), develop defensive strategies for targets facing an adversarial raid, determine fair value (so that shareholders cannot later challenge the price), finance mergers by providing a funding package, and run arbitrage operations (risk-free simultaneous buying and selling; in takeovers, speculation on likely targets is called risk arbitrage).

Costs and benefits (courseware): the benefit of a merger to firm A is PV(AB) minus (PV(A) + PV(B)). Cash compensation: cost = cash paid - PV(B); NPV to A = benefit - cost = PV(AB) - PV(A) - cash; NPV to B = cash - PV(B). Stock compensation: if the target holders receive a fraction alpha of the combined firm, cost = alpha x PV(AB) - PV(B), where alpha = new shares issued / (shares of acquirer + new shares issued); the apparent cost (shares issued x acquirer price) understates the true cost because the target holders share in the gains. With stock, the cost depends on the gains realised in the merger; with cash it does not.

Cash versus stock (courseware): four criteria decide the form of payment. Overvaluation: if the acquirer stock is overvalued relative to the target, paying in stock is cheaper. Taxes: cash is taxable to the target shareholders, stock exchange is generally not taxed immediately. Sharing of risks and rewards: with stock, the target holders share in the risks and rewards of the merger; with cash they do not. Discipline: the evidence is that cash-financed purchases are more successful than stock-financed ones, possibly because cash buyers are more disciplined.

Exchange ratio (courseware): the number of acquirer shares offered for each target share (also called the swap ratio). Bases: book value per share (ratio of the book values, objective but subject to accounting policy and ignoring inflation, so book values and economic values can differ); earnings per share (ratio of EPS; ignores unequal growth, one-off items, risks and negative earnings); market price per share (ratio of prices; a competitive and current measure but can be influenced by people with a stake in the outcome and thin trading); dividend discount value per share (ratio of DD values; useful where dividend streams are reasonable); and discounted cash flow value per share, equal to (firm value by DCF - debt value) / number of equity shares (ratio of DCF values; needs five to ten years of fairly firm business plans and ignores existing options).

Purchase of a division or plant (courseware): the buyer values the status quo business, the value of control and the value of synergy. Status quo value uses DCF (explicit forecast period of five to ten years, then a horizon value in steady state, both discounted to the present) or market multiples (value comparable assets alike, for example using the market value to NOPAT multiple of comparable firms). Value of control = value of the firm if optimally managed - value with current management; it is large when the company is badly managed. Synergy can come from lower overheads and shared costs, faster growth, longer growth period from competitive advantage, lower cost of capital from higher debt capacity and more efficient use of tax havens; it is easy to describe and hard to value. Valuation is prone to bias because each side wants to justify its view; a hostile bid shows this most, and the choices of return on capital, growth and cost of capital can be tailored to fit a figure.

Takeovers (courseware): control can be exercised by a stake smaller than 50 per cent (30 to 40 per cent if the remaining shareholders are dispersed and poorly organised). Methods: open market purchase (the usual start of a hostile takeover), negotiated acquisition from one or more current owners (usually promoters), and preferential allotment (a friendly route that gives the acquirer a strategic position and brings in finance). Arguments: supporters say takeovers improve management quality, discipline weak managers, enable synergy and protect small shareholders; critics say managers focus on size and short-term gain, that raiders are motivated by a quick profit, and that managers have responsibilities to society; research quoted in the courseware finds that target shareholders gain and bidding shareholders do not lose. Principles of regulation: transparency of the process, protection of minority shareholders (an equitable exit price for the other holders), realisation of economic gains (leeway to restructure), no undue concentration of market power, and financial support for capable bidders from financial institutions or the capital market. The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) measures concentration as the sum of the squares of the market shares, in percentage points.

SEBI takeover code and defences (courseware): the code covers disclosure by an acquirer once holdings cross a stated percentage, a trigger point after which a public offer is required, appointment of a merchant banker responsible for the offer, a public announcement, an offer price set by pricing guidelines (the highest of several reference prices), an escrow deposit to ensure payment, obligations of the target board during the offer period (it may not dispose of assets or issue capital without shareholder approval), the possibility of competing bids, and rules on creeping acquisition (limited annual increases in holdings without an open offer). The specific percentages, days and pricing formulae are not taught. Pre-offer defences: staggered board, super-majority clause, poison pills (the right to buy shares or bonds on favourable terms after a merger), poison puts (redeemable bonds that can be put on a takeover), dual-class shares and golden parachutes. Post-offer defences: greenmail (target buys back the bidder shares at a premium), Pacman defence (the target bids for the bidder), litigation, restructuring of assets (selling the crown jewels) and restructuring of liabilities. Indian defences listed: preferential allotment to promoters, creeping enhancement of holding, forming an amalgamated group of companies, selling the crown jewels and seeking a white knight.

Leveraged buyouts and acquisition financing (courseware): in a leveraged buyout (LBO) control of a company or business unit is bought mainly with debt; when management buys it is a management buyout (MBO), and afterwards the company usually becomes private. Debt gives management an incentive to improve cash flow (the discipline argument: debt is a sword, equity a pillow). Value is created through operational improvement, cash flow used to pay down debt (raising the equity share of enterprise value) and the tax shield on interest. A good candidate has a good management team, consistent cash flows, scope to improve operating efficiency, assets that can be sold off, low capital expenditure needs and an easy exit. Acquisition finance in India: the acquirer may use an overseas special purpose subsidiary to receive the loan; lenders look at the cash flow of the acquirer; the courseware indicates typical debt of three to six times EBITDA and a cost about 200 basis points above normal financing, depending on quality of products and management, regulation and viability of the cash flows.

Business alliances (courseware): alternatives to merger include joint ventures, strategic alliances, equity partnerships, licensing, franchising and network alliances. Rationale: sharing risk and resources (pooling know-how and capital in high technology), entering emerging markets through a partner sales force or channels, reducing expenditure (shared facilities), a more favourable view from regulators than a merger, and as a basis to acquire or exit a business. Success factors: complementary strengths, an expense too large for one firm, ability to work together on shared goals, a clear understanding of purpose, roles and obligations, fair sharing of responsibilities and benefits, and comparable time horizons and financial expectations.

Managing acquisitions (courseware): many mergers fail to create value, often because of people and culture. Collective wisdom: mergers are more attractive when the stock market is performing well; acquirers usually pay excessive prices, which benefits target shareholders; CEOs can fall in love with a deal; repeat acquirers do better than occasional ones; buying private companies tends to give higher returns than buying listed ones; connected (related) acquisitions yield higher returns than unrelated ones; integration is hard. Five sins: wandering too far from the core; striving for greatness (size over value); plunging without thinking (overstated intangibles, window-dressed statements, ignored contingent liabilities); overpaying (the winner curse in bidding contests); and inability to integrate. A disciplined programme: focus on the right targets (screen using criteria and a database), estimate synergies accurately, negotiate in a disciplined manner (with one team valuing the target and another doing the negotiation, and a walk-away price), and plan and control the integration. Premiums range from 20 to 60 per cent of the pre-acquisition market value.

Divestitures: motives, forms and financial evaluation (courseware): motives are focus on the most important businesses, insufficient contribution of a division to income, a business too large to manage, and an immediate need for funds. Sell-off motives: raising capital, reducing monetary losses, strategic alignment, focus, and the idea that a unit may be worth more as part of another company. A spin-off gives existing shareholders shares in the new company in the same proportion as before, with no change in ownership. A split-up divides the company into several new independent companies and the parent ceases to exist. An equity carve-out sells part of the subsidiary equity to new investors, raising cash for the parent, which keeps control; in a spin-off no cash is raised. Financial evaluation of a sell-off, step by step: (1) estimate the after-tax cash flows of the division; (2) set a discount rate reflecting the risk of the division (using firms in the same line of business as a proxy); (3) find the present value of the division; (4) find the market value of the division-specific liabilities, since their value may differ from book value; (5) value of ownership position (VOP) = value of the division - value of its liabilities; (6) compare with the divestiture proceeds (DP): if DP > VOP sell, if DP = VOP be indifferent, if DP < VOP keep the division. Tax: the courseware describes slump-sale capital gains treatment, which is not taught.

Holding companies and demergers (courseware): a holding company owns the equity of other companies to exert influence; it need not own all of it, and control can be exercised with a stake as small as 25 per cent where the holder manages its relationship with other shareholders. Benefits: central control, flexibility for growth, continuity and succession planning, tax planning, risk mitigation, legal protection of group assets and optimum use of funds. A demerger transfers one or more undertakings of a company to another company; the demerged company transfers, the resulting company receives. A demerger differs from a spin-off in that it is a legal scheme of arrangement; a spin-off and a split-up are forms of it. Family businesses use demergers to divide a business empire and solve succession. Conditions for tax-neutral treatment in the courseware: the resulting company takes all the assets and liabilities of the transferred undertaking at the book values of the demerged company, issues shares to the shareholders of the demerged company on a proportional basis, and a required proportion of shareholders move to the resulting company (the proportion is not taught).

payload.title: Types of mergers, acquisitions and takeovers
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Type | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Horizontal merger** | Firms in the **same market** combine: **larger market share**, possible **near-monopoly** |
| **Vertical merger** | **Buyer and seller** (supplier and customer) combine |
| **Conglomerate merger** | **Unconnected businesses**; gains come from **financial resources, debt capacity, management** |
| **Congeneric merger** | Firms **connected** by technology, products or markets |
| **Reverse merger** | A **smaller unlisted** firm acquires a **larger listed** one, avoiding a lengthy **public issue** |

**Acquisition:** purchase of a **controlling interest** (by agreement, fresh shares, open market, cash plus shares, or a general offer). **Slump sale:** a business sold for **one lump sum** without values for each asset. **Purchase of a division or plant:** only **part** of a firm is bought. **Takeover:** acquiring a stake, typically **50 to 100 per cent**, to gain **control**; **friendly** if the target management agrees, **hostile** if not. **Leveraged buyout:** a takeover **financed mainly by debt**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: In a merger two firms become one; in an acquisition one firm buys control of another that may continue as a separate company.

payload.title: Why firms merge: synergy and economies
payload.core_explanation_md:

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Buying a ready business can be faster than building plant and hiring staff from scratch.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the condition for synergy in a merger of A and B?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The combined value is greater than the sum of the separate values.

payload.title: Dubious reasons for merging
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Diversification:** investors can **diversify cheaply** by holding shares in both firms, so a merger adds **no value for them**. **Exceptions:** a firm facing **bankruptcy** that only a merger can save, and a firm whose **owners cannot diversify** by themselves.

**Lower financing costs:** each firm creditors become a **guarantor of the other**, so **shareholders bear extra risk**; in an efficient market the **lower cost of debt is offset by a higher cost of equity**.

**Growth in earnings per share:** the **P/E ratio of the combined firm falls**, so its **market value is the sum of the separate values** and the rise in **EPS is an illusion**. Only an **inefficient** market can be fooled.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Earnings per share can rise through a merger even though no value has been created.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does a rise in EPS after a merger not prove value was created?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The price-earnings ratio of the combined firm falls, so market value stays at the sum of the separate values.

payload.title: How an amalgamation proceeds, and the regulators
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Regulators:** the **Companies Act** (main law; **NCLT** sanctions the scheme), **SEBI** (protects **minority shareholders**), the **Competition Commission** (protects **consumers** from reduced competition; combinations above specified limits must be **notified**).

**Sequence:** review **object clauses** -> inform **stock exchanges** -> **board approvals** of the draft scheme -> **application to the NCLT** -> **notice** to shareholders and creditors -> **meetings** where a prescribed majority in value must approve -> **petition to the NCLT** to confirm -> file the order with the **Registrar** -> **transfer of assets and liabilities** -> **issue of shares and debentures**, after which trading begins.

**Investment bankers** arrange mergers, develop **defences**, determine **fair value**, **finance** the deal and run **arbitrage**. The specific majorities, notice periods and thresholds are **not taught** here.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Fair value matters because shareholders can challenge a price that is not reasonable.

self_check.prompt_text: Which body sanctions an amalgamation scheme?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The National Company Law Tribunal.

payload.title: Tax and accounting for business combinations
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Tax:** a qualifying amalgamation lets the combined firm claim certain **deductions** and **carry forward unabsorbed losses and depreciation**; **stamp duty** is a **state** levy. Conditions and figures are **not taught**.

**Accounting under Ind AS 103: acquisition method**

1. **Identify the acquirer.**
2. Determine the **acquisition date**.
3. **Recognise and measure** identifiable assets, liabilities and any **non-controlling interest** at **fair value**.
4. Recognise **goodwill** or a **gain on a bargain purchase**.

**Common control combinations** (the same party controls all combining entities before and after): the **pooling of interests** method uses **carrying amounts**, makes **no fair value adjustments**, and adjusts the **difference in capital** from the share exchange in **reserves**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Under pooling no new goodwill appears, because values are not restated.

self_check.prompt_text: Which method applies to a business combination under common control?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The pooling of interests method.

payload.title: Merger gain and cost with cash compensation
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Benefit** = **PV(AB) - (PV(A) + PV(B))**.

**Cash:** **cost = cash paid - PV(B)**; **NPV to A = benefit - cost = PV(AB) - PV(A) - cash**; **NPV to B = cash - PV(B)**.

Example pattern: if the total gain is **Rs 25 crore** and A pays **Rs 5 crore above B stand-alone value**, A keeps **Rs 20 crore** and B gets **Rs 5 crore**. The gain is **shared**; **a higher price moves gain from A to B**.

Stand-alone value of the acquirer
Cash paid to the target holders

assumptions: Cash paid is certain and independent of the merger gain
Values are present values
common_errors: Comparing cash with the target market price instead of its stand-alone value
Forgetting that the cash paid is the acquirer cost

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The seller gains only if the cash exceeds its stand-alone value.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the cost of a cash merger to the acquirer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The cash paid minus the stand-alone value of the target.

payload.title: Merger cost with stock compensation
payload.core_explanation_md:
Target holders receive a **fraction alpha of the combined firm**: **alpha = new shares issued / (acquirer shares + new shares issued)**.

**True cost = alpha x PV(AB) - PV(B)**, where **PV(AB) = PV(A) + PV(B) + benefit**.

The **apparent cost** (**shares issued x acquirer price**, minus PV(B)) **understates** the true cost because target holders **share in the gain**. **NPV to A = benefit - cost**; **NPV to B = cost**.

**With stock, the cost depends on the merger gain; with cash it does not.**

variables.name: Fraction of the combined firm owned by target holders
Value of the combined firm including the benefit
Stand-alone value of the target

assumptions: Shares are valued at their pre-merger market values
The benefit is shared in proportion to ownership
common_errors: Using the pre-merger share price to compute cost and ignoring the gain
Dividing new shares by the old share count only

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Paying in stock shares the risk that the benefit will not materialise.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the apparent cost of a stock deal too low?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the target holders also own part of the merger gain.

payload.title: Cash or stock as payment
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Criterion | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Overvaluation** | If the acquirer stock is **overvalued**, **stock** is the cheaper payment |
| **Taxes** | **Cash** is **taxable** to target holders; a **share exchange** is generally **not taxed at once** |
| **Sharing of risks and rewards** | **Stock** lets target holders **share** risks and rewards; **cash** does not |
| **Discipline** | **Cash-financed** purchases have **done better** than stock-financed ones, possibly because cash buyers are **more disciplined** |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A cash buyer bears the whole risk and so scrutinises the price more closely.

self_check.prompt_text: When is paying in stock the cheaper option for the acquirer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When the acquirer shares are overvalued.

payload.title: Exchange ratio and its bases
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Exchange (swap) ratio = acquirer shares offered per target share.** A ratio of **0.5** means **one acquirer share for every two target shares**.

**Ratio on a basis = value per share of the target / value per share of the acquirer**, using:

- **Book value per share**: objective, but **accounting policies and inflation** distort it.
- **Earnings per share**: ignores **unequal growth, one-off items, risk and negative earnings**.
- **Market price per share**: **current and competitive**, but **thin trading** or interested parties can distort it.
- **Dividend discount value**: suits firms with **reasonable dividend streams**.
- **DCF value per share** = (**DCF firm value - debt**) / **shares**: needs **five to ten years** of sound plans.

**New shares to issue = ratio x target shares.**

variables.name: Value per share of the target on the chosen basis
Value per share of the acquirer on the same basis

assumptions: Same basis for both firms
Values are per equity share
common_errors: Dividing the acquirer value by the target value
Mixing bases for the two firms

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Different bases give different ratios, so the final ratio is a negotiated figure.

self_check.prompt_text: What does an exchange ratio of 0.5 mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The acquirer offers one share for every two target shares.

payload.title: Valuing a division or plant to be bought
payload.core_explanation_md:
The buyer values **three layers**:

1. **Status quo value** by **DCF** (an **explicit forecast** of five to ten years, then a **horizon value** in steady state, both discounted) or by **market multiples** of comparable assets (for example **value to NOPAT**).
2. **Value of control** = **value if optimally managed - value under current management**; large when the business is **badly run**.
3. **Value of synergy**: lower **overheads**, faster or **longer growth**, **lower cost of capital** from more debt capacity, better use of **tax**; **easy to describe, hard to value**.

**Bias:** each side wants to **justify its view**; the choice of **growth, return on capital and discount rate** can be tailored to reach a figure, especially in a **hostile** bid.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Control is worth nothing if the firm is already managed as well as it can be.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the value of control measured?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The value if optimally managed minus the value under current management.

payload.title: Takeovers: routes, arguments and regulation principles
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Control** can need **less than 50 per cent** (**30 to 40 per cent** if other holders are dispersed).

**Routes:** **open market purchase** (usual start of a **hostile** bid), **negotiated purchase** from promoters, **preferential allotment** (friendly; gives a **strategic stake** and brings in **funds**).

**For:** better **management quality**, **discipline** on weak managers, **synergy**, protection of **small holders**. **Against:** a focus on **size** and **short-term gain**, **raiders** seeking a quick profit, duty to **society**. **Research** quoted: **target holders gain**, bidders do **not lose**.

**Principles of regulation:** **transparency**, **minority protection** (equitable exit price), **freedom to realise economic gains**, **no undue concentration of market power**, and **financial support** for capable bidders.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A hostile takeover often starts with quiet purchases of shares on the market.

self_check.prompt_text: Which takeover route is friendly and can bring funds into the target?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A preferential allotment of shares to the acquirer.

payload.title: Market concentration: the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index
payload.core_explanation_md:
**HHI = the sum of the squares of the market shares**, with shares in **percentage points**.

Example pattern: **three firms with 20 per cent each and ten with 4 per cent each** give **3 x 400 + 10 x 16 = 1,360**. A market with **one firm at 52 per cent and twelve at 4 per cent** gives **2,704 + 192 = 2,896**.

The index **rises with both inequality of shares and fewer firms**, so regulators use it to judge whether a merger **concentrates market power** too much.

variables.name: Market share of firm i
Number of firms

assumptions: Shares are expressed in percentage points
All firms in the market are included
common_errors: Adding shares instead of squares
Using fractions instead of percentage points and mixing scales

payload.expanded_explanation_md: A single firm with 100 per cent share gives the maximum value of 10,000.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does a merger of two large rivals raise the HHI?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Their shares add and the squared sum is larger than the sum of the separate squares.

payload.title: Takeover code principles and anti-takeover defences
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Takeover code (principles only; percentages, days and formulae are not taught):** **disclosure** once holdings cross a stated level; a **trigger point** after which a **public offer** must be made; a **merchant banker** responsible for the offer; a **public announcement**; an **offer price** from **pricing guidelines**; an **escrow** deposit to **ensure payment**; **target board restrictions** during the offer; **competing bids**; limits on **creeping acquisition**.

**Pre-offer defences:** **staggered board**, **super-majority clause**, **poison pill**, **poison put**, **dual-class shares**, **golden parachute**.

**Post-offer defences:** **greenmail**, **Pacman defence**, **litigation**, **selling the crown jewels**, **restructuring liabilities**.

**Indian list:** **preferential allotment to promoters**, **creeping enhancement**, **amalgamated group**, **selling crown jewels**, **a white knight**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A white knight is a friendly rescuer that buys the target on better terms than the hostile bidder.

self_check.prompt_text: What is greenmail?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The target buys back the bidder shares at a premium in return for the bidder giving up the takeover.

payload.title: Leveraged buyouts and acquisition financing
payload.core_explanation_md:
**LBO:** a company or unit is bought **mainly with debt**; a **management buyout (MBO)** is one where **management buys**. Afterwards the firm usually becomes **private**.

**Debt disciplines:** it forces **cash flow improvement**. In the courseware phrase, **debt is a sword, equity a pillow**.

**Value is created by:** **operating improvement**, **cash flow repaying debt** (raising the **equity share** of enterprise value) and the **interest tax shield**.

**Good LBO candidate:** **good management**, **steady cash flows**, **room to improve efficiency**, **assets that can be sold**, **low capital expenditure** needs and an **easy exit**.

**Acquisition finance:** lenders look at the **cash flow of the acquirer**; the courseware indicates **debt of three to six times EBITDA** at a cost **above normal financing**, depending on product and management quality, regulation and cash flow viability.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The risk is that heavy fixed charges can sink the firm if cash flow disappoints.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the three sources of value in a leveraged buyout.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Operating improvement, debt paydown from cash flow and the interest tax shield.

payload.title: Business alliances as an alternative to merger
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Forms:** **joint ventures**, **strategic alliances**, **equity partnerships**, **licensing**, **franchising** and **network alliances**.

**Why:** **share risk and resources** (especially in **high technology**), **enter emerging markets** through a partner **channels**, **reduce expenditure** by sharing facilities, a **more favourable view from regulators** than a merger, and a **route to acquire or exit** a business.

**Success factors:** **complementary strengths**, a cost **too large for one firm**, ability to **work together**, clear **purpose, roles and obligations**, **fair sharing** of responsibilities and benefits, and comparable **time horizons** and **financial expectations**.

payload.title: Managing acquisitions: five sins and a disciplined programme
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Many deals fail to create value**, often over **people and culture**.

**Collective wisdom:** deals cluster when **markets are strong**; **buyers usually overpay**; **repeat acquirers** do better; **private targets** and **related** acquisitions do better; **integration is hard**.

**Five sins:** **wandering too far from the core**; **striving for greatness** (size over value); **plunging without thinking** (overstated intangibles, window-dressed statements, ignored contingent liabilities); **overpaying** (the **winner curse**); **inability to integrate**.

**Disciplined programme:** focus on the **right targets** (screening criteria and a database), **estimate synergies accurately**, **negotiate with discipline** (one team values, another negotiates; set a **walk-away price**) and **plan and control integration**. Premiums run **20 to 60 per cent** of pre-bid market value (courseware range).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Synergy that is only assumed, never planned, usually does not appear.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The highest bidder is often the one that most overestimated the value, so it overpays.

payload.title: Divestitures: forms and motives
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Divestiture** is the opposite of acquisition: a **smaller asset base and less control**.

| Form | Key feature |
| --- | --- |
| **Partial sell-off** | A part of the business sold to another firm |
| **Transfer of ownership** | An investor sells an **equity stake or controlling block** |
| **Spin-off** | **Existing shareholders get shares** of the new company **pro rata**; **ownership unchanged**; **no cash raised** |
| **Split-up** | The company divides into **several independent companies**; the **parent ceases to exist** |
| **Equity carve-out** | **Part of the subsidiary equity is sold to new investors**; **cash comes in**; the **parent keeps control** |
| **Demerger** | A **legal scheme** moving undertakings to a **resulting company** |
| **PSU disinvestment** | **Government** stake transferred by **privatisation** |

**Motives:** **focus**, a division that **contributes too little**, a business **too large to manage**, **need for funds**, **strategic fit**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A spin-off gives shareholders new shares; a carve-out sells shares for cash.

self_check.prompt_text: Which divestiture raises cash while the parent keeps control?
self_check.expected_takeaway: An equity carve-out.

payload.title: Financial evaluation of a sell-off
payload.core_explanation_md:
1. Estimate the **after-tax cash flows** of the division.
2. Choose a **discount rate for the division risk** (use firms in the **same line of business** as proxy).
3. Compute the **present value of the division**.
4. Find the **market value of the division-specific liabilities** (may differ from book value).
5. **VOP (value of ownership position) = value of the division - value of its liabilities.**
6. Compare with the **divestiture proceeds (DP)**.

**Decision rule:** **DP > VOP: sell**; **DP = VOP: indifferent**; **DP < VOP: keep.**

Market value of the division-specific liabilities

assumptions: Discount rate reflects the division risk
Liabilities are valued at market, not book
common_errors: Using book value of liabilities
Using the parent discount rate for a division of different risk

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The parent sells only when the proceeds beat what the division is worth to it.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Keep the division.

payload.title: Holding companies and demergers
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Holding company:** owns **equity in other companies** to **control** them; **full ownership is not needed**, and control may be possible with **as little as 25 per cent** if relations with other holders are managed (courseware).

**Benefits:** **central control**, **flexibility for growth**, **succession planning**, **tax planning**, **risk mitigation**, **legal protection of group assets**, **optimum use of funds**.

**Demerger:** a **legal scheme** moving **one or more undertakings** into a **resulting company**; the **demerged company** transfers. **Family groups** use it to **divide a business empire** and solve **succession**.

**Tax-neutral demerger (courseware conditions):** the resulting company takes **all assets and liabilities** of the undertaking **at the book values** of the demerged company, issues **shares to the demerged company shareholders in proportion**, and a **required proportion** of shareholders move across (**not taught**).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: In a demerger the shareholders end up holding shares in both companies.

self_check.expected_takeaway: It receives the transferred undertaking and issues shares to the demerged company shareholders.

items.title: Types of mergers, acquisitions and takeovers
items.core_explanation_md:
| Type | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Horizontal merger** | Firms in the **same market** combine: **larger market share**, possible **near-monopoly** |
| **Vertical merger** | **Buyer and seller** (supplier and customer) combine |
| **Conglomerate merger** | **Unconnected businesses**; gains come from **financial resources, debt capacity, management** |
| **Congeneric merger** | Firms **connected** by technology, products or markets |
| **Reverse merger** | A **smaller unlisted** firm acquires a **larger listed** one, avoiding a lengthy **public issue** |

**Acquisition:** purchase of a **controlling interest** (by agreement, fresh shares, open market, cash plus shares, or a general offer). **Slump sale:** a business sold for **one lump sum** without values for each asset. **Purchase of a division or plant:** only **part** of a firm is bought. **Takeover:** acquiring a stake, typically **50 to 100 per cent**, to gain **control**; **friendly** if the target management agrees, **hostile** if not. **Leveraged buyout:** a takeover **financed mainly by debt**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: In a merger two firms become one; in an acquisition one firm buys control of another that may continue as a separate company.

self_check.expected_takeaway: A vertical merger.

items.title: Why firms merge: synergy and economies
items.core_explanation_md:
**Synergy:** the combined value exceeds the separate values, **V(AB) > V(A) + V(B)**.

**Real gains:** **operating economies** (**real** economies cut inputs per unit of output; **pecuniary** ones come from **cheaper factor prices**), **economies of scale and scope**, **vertical integration** (but **outsourcing** may be better), **complementary resources**, **faster growth** and shorter **time to market**, **market power** from fewer competitors, **tax** benefits such as set-off of losses, **use of surplus funds**, **managerial effectiveness** (a better team, and the **threat of takeover** disciplines managers) and **industry consolidation** where capacity is excessive.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Buying a ready business can be faster than building plant and hiring staff from scratch.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the condition for synergy in a merger of A and B?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The combined value is greater than the sum of the separate values.

items.title: Dubious reasons for merging
items.core_explanation_md:
**Diversification:** investors can **diversify cheaply** by holding shares in both firms, so a merger adds **no value for them**. **Exceptions:** a firm facing **bankruptcy** that only a merger can save, and a firm whose **owners cannot diversify** by themselves.

**Lower financing costs:** each firm creditors become a **guarantor of the other**, so **shareholders bear extra risk**; in an efficient market the **lower cost of debt is offset by a higher cost of equity**.

**Growth in earnings per share:** the **P/E ratio of the combined firm falls**, so its **market value is the sum of the separate values** and the rise in **EPS is an illusion**. Only an **inefficient** market can be fooled.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Earnings per share can rise through a merger even though no value has been created.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does a rise in EPS after a merger not prove value was created?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The price-earnings ratio of the combined firm falls, so market value stays at the sum of the separate values.

items.title: How an amalgamation proceeds, and the regulators
items.core_explanation_md:
**Regulators:** the **Companies Act** (main law; **NCLT** sanctions the scheme), **SEBI** (protects **minority shareholders**), the **Competition Commission** (protects **consumers** from reduced competition; combinations above specified limits must be **notified**).

**Sequence:** review **object clauses** -> inform **stock exchanges** -> **board approvals** of the draft scheme -> **application to the NCLT** -> **notice** to shareholders and creditors -> **meetings** where a prescribed majority in value must approve -> **petition to the NCLT** to confirm -> file the order with the **Registrar** -> **transfer of assets and liabilities** -> **issue of shares and debentures**, after which trading begins.

**Investment bankers** arrange mergers, develop **defences**, determine **fair value**, **finance** the deal and run **arbitrage**. The specific majorities, notice periods and thresholds are **not taught** here.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Fair value matters because shareholders can challenge a price that is not reasonable.

self_check.prompt_text: Which body sanctions an amalgamation scheme?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The National Company Law Tribunal.

items.title: Tax and accounting for business combinations
items.core_explanation_md:
**Tax:** a qualifying amalgamation lets the combined firm claim certain **deductions** and **carry forward unabsorbed losses and depreciation**; **stamp duty** is a **state** levy. Conditions and figures are **not taught**.

**Accounting under Ind AS 103: acquisition method**

1. **Identify the acquirer.**
2. Determine the **acquisition date**.
3. **Recognise and measure** identifiable assets, liabilities and any **non-controlling interest** at **fair value**.
4. Recognise **goodwill** or a **gain on a bargain purchase**.

**Common control combinations** (the same party controls all combining entities before and after): the **pooling of interests** method uses **carrying amounts**, makes **no fair value adjustments**, and adjusts the **difference in capital** from the share exchange in **reserves**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Under pooling no new goodwill appears, because values are not restated.

self_check.prompt_text: Which method applies to a business combination under common control?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The pooling of interests method.

items.title: Merger gain and cost with cash compensation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Benefit** = **PV(AB) - (PV(A) + PV(B))**.

**Cash:** **cost = cash paid - PV(B)**; **NPV to A = benefit - cost = PV(AB) - PV(A) - cash**; **NPV to B = cash - PV(B)**.

Example pattern: if the total gain is **Rs 25 crore** and A pays **Rs 5 crore above B stand-alone value**, A keeps **Rs 20 crore** and B gets **Rs 5 crore**. The gain is **shared**; **a higher price moves gain from A to B**.

Stand-alone value of the acquirer
Cash paid to the target holders

assumptions: Cash paid is certain and independent of the merger gain
Values are present values
common_errors: Comparing cash with the target market price instead of its stand-alone value
Forgetting that the cash paid is the acquirer cost

items.expanded_explanation_md: The seller gains only if the cash exceeds its stand-alone value.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the cost of a cash merger to the acquirer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The cash paid minus the stand-alone value of the target.

items.title: Merger cost with stock compensation
items.core_explanation_md:
Target holders receive a **fraction alpha of the combined firm**: **alpha = new shares issued / (acquirer shares + new shares issued)**.

**True cost = alpha x PV(AB) - PV(B)**, where **PV(AB) = PV(A) + PV(B) + benefit**.

The **apparent cost** (**shares issued x acquirer price**, minus PV(B)) **understates** the true cost because target holders **share in the gain**. **NPV to A = benefit - cost**; **NPV to B = cost**.

**With stock, the cost depends on the merger gain; with cash it does not.**

variables.name: Fraction of the combined firm owned by target holders
Value of the combined firm including the benefit
Stand-alone value of the target

assumptions: Shares are valued at their pre-merger market values
The benefit is shared in proportion to ownership
common_errors: Using the pre-merger share price to compute cost and ignoring the gain
Dividing new shares by the old share count only

items.expanded_explanation_md: Paying in stock shares the risk that the benefit will not materialise.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the apparent cost of a stock deal too low?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the target holders also own part of the merger gain.

items.title: Cash or stock as payment
items.core_explanation_md:
| Criterion | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Overvaluation** | If the acquirer stock is **overvalued**, **stock** is the cheaper payment |
| **Taxes** | **Cash** is **taxable** to target holders; a **share exchange** is generally **not taxed at once** |
| **Sharing of risks and rewards** | **Stock** lets target holders **share** risks and rewards; **cash** does not |
| **Discipline** | **Cash-financed** purchases have **done better** than stock-financed ones, possibly because cash buyers are **more disciplined** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: A cash buyer bears the whole risk and so scrutinises the price more closely.

self_check.expected_takeaway: When the acquirer shares are overvalued.

items.title: Exchange ratio and its bases
items.core_explanation_md:
**Exchange (swap) ratio = acquirer shares offered per target share.** A ratio of **0.5** means **one acquirer share for every two target shares**.

**Ratio on a basis = value per share of the target / value per share of the acquirer**, using:

- **Book value per share**: objective, but **accounting policies and inflation** distort it.
- **Earnings per share**: ignores **unequal growth, one-off items, risk and negative earnings**.
- **Market price per share**: **current and competitive**, but **thin trading** or interested parties can distort it.
- **Dividend discount value**: suits firms with **reasonable dividend streams**.
- **DCF value per share** = (**DCF firm value - debt**) / **shares**: needs **five to ten years** of sound plans.

**New shares to issue = ratio x target shares.**

variables.name: Value per share of the target on the chosen basis
Value per share of the acquirer on the same basis

assumptions: Same basis for both firms
Values are per equity share
common_errors: Dividing the acquirer value by the target value
Mixing bases for the two firms

items.expanded_explanation_md: Different bases give different ratios, so the final ratio is a negotiated figure.

self_check.prompt_text: What does an exchange ratio of 0.5 mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The acquirer offers one share for every two target shares.

items.title: Valuing a division or plant to be bought
items.core_explanation_md:
The buyer values **three layers**:

1. **Status quo value** by **DCF** (an **explicit forecast** of five to ten years, then a **horizon value** in steady state, both discounted) or by **market multiples** of comparable assets (for example **value to NOPAT**).
2. **Value of control** = **value if optimally managed - value under current management**; large when the business is **badly run**.
3. **Value of synergy**: lower **overheads**, faster or **longer growth**, **lower cost of capital** from more debt capacity, better use of **tax**; **easy to describe, hard to value**.

**Bias:** each side wants to **justify its view**; the choice of **growth, return on capital and discount rate** can be tailored to reach a figure, especially in a **hostile** bid.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Control is worth nothing if the firm is already managed as well as it can be.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the value of control measured?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The value if optimally managed minus the value under current management.

items.title: Takeovers: routes, arguments and regulation principles
items.core_explanation_md:
**Control** can need **less than 50 per cent** (**30 to 40 per cent** if other holders are dispersed).

**Routes:** **open market purchase** (usual start of a **hostile** bid), **negotiated purchase** from promoters, **preferential allotment** (friendly; gives a **strategic stake** and brings in **funds**).

**For:** better **management quality**, **discipline** on weak managers, **synergy**, protection of **small holders**. **Against:** a focus on **size** and **short-term gain**, **raiders** seeking a quick profit, duty to **society**. **Research** quoted: **target holders gain**, bidders do **not lose**.

**Principles of regulation:** **transparency**, **minority protection** (equitable exit price), **freedom to realise economic gains**, **no undue concentration of market power**, and **financial support** for capable bidders.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A hostile takeover often starts with quiet purchases of shares on the market.

self_check.prompt_text: Which takeover route is friendly and can bring funds into the target?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A preferential allotment of shares to the acquirer.

items.title: Market concentration: the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index
items.core_explanation_md:
**HHI = the sum of the squares of the market shares**, with shares in **percentage points**.

Example pattern: **three firms with 20 per cent each and ten with 4 per cent each** give **3 x 400 + 10 x 16 = 1,360**. A market with **one firm at 52 per cent and twelve at 4 per cent** gives **2,704 + 192 = 2,896**.

The index **rises with both inequality of shares and fewer firms**, so regulators use it to judge whether a merger **concentrates market power** too much.

Number of firms

assumptions: Shares are expressed in percentage points
All firms in the market are included
common_errors: Adding shares instead of squares
Using fractions instead of percentage points and mixing scales

items.expanded_explanation_md: A single firm with 100 per cent share gives the maximum value of 10,000.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does a merger of two large rivals raise the HHI?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Their shares add and the squared sum is larger than the sum of the separate squares.

items.title: Takeover code principles and anti-takeover defences
items.core_explanation_md:
**Takeover code (principles only; percentages, days and formulae are not taught):** **disclosure** once holdings cross a stated level; a **trigger point** after which a **public offer** must be made; a **merchant banker** responsible for the offer; a **public announcement**; an **offer price** from **pricing guidelines**; an **escrow** deposit to **ensure payment**; **target board restrictions** during the offer; **competing bids**; limits on **creeping acquisition**.

**Pre-offer defences:** **staggered board**, **super-majority clause**, **poison pill**, **poison put**, **dual-class shares**, **golden parachute**.

**Post-offer defences:** **greenmail**, **Pacman defence**, **litigation**, **selling the crown jewels**, **restructuring liabilities**.

**Indian list:** **preferential allotment to promoters**, **creeping enhancement**, **amalgamated group**, **selling crown jewels**, **a white knight**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A white knight is a friendly rescuer that buys the target on better terms than the hostile bidder.

self_check.prompt_text: What is greenmail?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The target buys back the bidder shares at a premium in return for the bidder giving up the takeover.

items.title: Leveraged buyouts and acquisition financing
items.core_explanation_md:
**LBO:** a company or unit is bought **mainly with debt**; a **management buyout (MBO)** is one where **management buys**. Afterwards the firm usually becomes **private**.

**Debt disciplines:** it forces **cash flow improvement**. In the courseware phrase, **debt is a sword, equity a pillow**.

**Value is created by:** **operating improvement**, **cash flow repaying debt** (raising the **equity share** of enterprise value) and the **interest tax shield**.

**Good LBO candidate:** **good management**, **steady cash flows**, **room to improve efficiency**, **assets that can be sold**, **low capital expenditure** needs and an **easy exit**.

**Acquisition finance:** lenders look at the **cash flow of the acquirer**; the courseware indicates **debt of three to six times EBITDA** at a cost **above normal financing**, depending on product and management quality, regulation and cash flow viability.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The risk is that heavy fixed charges can sink the firm if cash flow disappoints.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the three sources of value in a leveraged buyout.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Operating improvement, debt paydown from cash flow and the interest tax shield.

items.title: Business alliances as an alternative to merger
items.core_explanation_md:
**Forms:** **joint ventures**, **strategic alliances**, **equity partnerships**, **licensing**, **franchising** and **network alliances**.

**Why:** **share risk and resources** (especially in **high technology**), **enter emerging markets** through a partner **channels**, **reduce expenditure** by sharing facilities, a **more favourable view from regulators** than a merger, and a **route to acquire or exit** a business.

**Success factors:** **complementary strengths**, a cost **too large for one firm**, ability to **work together**, clear **purpose, roles and obligations**, **fair sharing** of responsibilities and benefits, and comparable **time horizons** and **financial expectations**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: An alliance can be a trial before a full merger.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two success factors for a business alliance.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example complementary strengths and a fair sharing of benefits and responsibilities.

items.title: Managing acquisitions: five sins and a disciplined programme
items.core_explanation_md:
**Many deals fail to create value**, often over **people and culture**.

**Collective wisdom:** deals cluster when **markets are strong**; **buyers usually overpay**; **repeat acquirers** do better; **private targets** and **related** acquisitions do better; **integration is hard**.

**Five sins:** **wandering too far from the core**; **striving for greatness** (size over value); **plunging without thinking** (overstated intangibles, window-dressed statements, ignored contingent liabilities); **overpaying** (the **winner curse**); **inability to integrate**.

**Disciplined programme:** focus on the **right targets** (screening criteria and a database), **estimate synergies accurately**, **negotiate with discipline** (one team values, another negotiates; set a **walk-away price**) and **plan and control integration**. Premiums run **20 to 60 per cent** of pre-bid market value (courseware range).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Synergy that is only assumed, never planned, usually does not appear.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the winner curse?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The highest bidder is often the one that most overestimated the value, so it overpays.

items.title: Divestitures: forms and motives
items.core_explanation_md:
**Divestiture** is the opposite of acquisition: a **smaller asset base and less control**.

| Form | Key feature |
| --- | --- |
| **Partial sell-off** | A part of the business sold to another firm |
| **Transfer of ownership** | An investor sells an **equity stake or controlling block** |
| **Spin-off** | **Existing shareholders get shares** of the new company **pro rata**; **ownership unchanged**; **no cash raised** |
| **Split-up** | The company divides into **several independent companies**; the **parent ceases to exist** |
| **Equity carve-out** | **Part of the subsidiary equity is sold to new investors**; **cash comes in**; the **parent keeps control** |
| **Demerger** | A **legal scheme** moving undertakings to a **resulting company** |
| **PSU disinvestment** | **Government** stake transferred by **privatisation** |

**Motives:** **focus**, a division that **contributes too little**, a business **too large to manage**, **need for funds**, **strategic fit**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A spin-off gives shareholders new shares; a carve-out sells shares for cash.

self_check.prompt_text: Which divestiture raises cash while the parent keeps control?
self_check.expected_takeaway: An equity carve-out.

items.title: Financial evaluation of a sell-off
items.core_explanation_md:
1. Estimate the **after-tax cash flows** of the division.
2. Choose a **discount rate for the division risk** (use firms in the **same line of business** as proxy).
3. Compute the **present value of the division**.
4. Find the **market value of the division-specific liabilities** (may differ from book value).
5. **VOP (value of ownership position) = value of the division - value of its liabilities.**
6. Compare with the **divestiture proceeds (DP)**.

**Decision rule:** **DP > VOP: sell**; **DP = VOP: indifferent**; **DP < VOP: keep.**

Market value of the division-specific liabilities

assumptions: Discount rate reflects the division risk
Liabilities are valued at market, not book
common_errors: Using book value of liabilities
Using the parent discount rate for a division of different risk

items.expanded_explanation_md: The parent sells only when the proceeds beat what the division is worth to it.

self_check.prompt_text: If divestiture proceeds are below VOP, what should the parent do?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Keep the division.

items.title: Holding companies and demergers
items.core_explanation_md:
**Holding company:** owns **equity in other companies** to **control** them; **full ownership is not needed**, and control may be possible with **as little as 25 per cent** if relations with other holders are managed (courseware).

**Benefits:** **central control**, **flexibility for growth**, **succession planning**, **tax planning**, **risk mitigation**, **legal protection of group assets**, **optimum use of funds**.

**Demerger:** a **legal scheme** moving **one or more undertakings** into a **resulting company**; the **demerged company** transfers. **Family groups** use it to **divide a business empire** and solve **succession**.

**Tax-neutral demerger (courseware conditions):** the resulting company takes **all assets and liabilities** of the undertaking **at the book values** of the demerged company, issues **shares to the demerged company shareholders in proportion**, and a **required proportion** of shareholders move across (**not taught**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: In a demerger the shareholders end up holding shares in both companies.

self_check.expected_takeaway: It receives the transferred undertaking and issues shares to the demerged company shareholders.
